chunks: And that which was narrated - Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Hajj of the 'Sarurah' (one who cannot perform Hajj for themselves) suffices for him and for the one for whom he performs Hajj. This does not contradict what we mentioned, because it is not impossible that his saying (peace be upon him) 'suffices for him' applies as long as he is poor and has no wealth; but when he becomes wealthy, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him according to what the first report contained. And we said this because it is ambiguous and permissible [of multiple interpretations], while the first report is detailed, and the ruling is applied to the ambiguous [report] first.
And that which was narrated: -(1433) 79 - Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar from Bakr ibn Salih who said:

I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that my son is with me and I have ordered him to perform Hajj on behalf of my mother; will it suffice for her as the Hajj of Islam? He wrote (peace be upon him): 'No, and his son was a 'Sarurah' and his mother was a 'Sarurah'.'

So this report is also interpreted to mean that if the son has wealth, it is not permissible for him to perform Hajj on her behalf until he has performed Hajj for himself, or he gives [the cost to a] 'Sarurah' who has no wealth, according to what we preceded. And this interpretation is not invalidated by what was narrated:

key_terms.حَجَّة الْإِسْلَام: The obligatory Hajj that every Muslim must perform once in their lifetime.
key_terms.صَرُورَة: A person who is unable to perform Hajj for themselves, often due to poverty or inability.
key_terms.مُجْمَل: Ambiguous or general text that requires interpretation.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling of Hajj for a 'Sarurah' and does it suffice for both the performer and the represented person?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi employs the principle of reconciling apparent contradictions by distinguishing between the general permissibility of a poor person's Hajj sufficing for both parties and the specific obligation of performing one's own Hajj al-Islam first if capable. He clarifies that the report where the son’s Hajj for his mother does not suffice is contextualized to cases where the son has wealth, thereby requiring him to fulfill his primary duty before acting as a proxy, or to transfer the financial burden to another indigent pilgrim. This nuanced interpretation preserves the integrity of the primary obligation while accommodating the realities of economic capacity within Shia jurisprudence.
